deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 29 belongs to a set of lecture notes on ancient history, specifically the geography and monuments of Egypt. The previous and next pages are on the same subject.

The page continues the description of the Labyrinth begun on folio 28:
- Its 12 halls are interpreted as the 12 signs of the zodiac.
- Half of them lie 'above' and half 'below' the equator, mirroring the earlier statement that half the rooms were above ground and half below.
- The whole temple holds 3000 chambers and is said to be the work of a king (the name is uncertain).
- There are 360 niches, read as the 360 degrees of the zodiac.

It then treats III. Obelisks. All are of granite and cut from a single piece. They vary in height; the tallest, still found in Rome, is 120 feet. Most are covered with skilfully engraved hieroglyphs.

Next comes the section on Lower Egypt. It was full of cities, with Sais as the capital. Sais had a temple of Minerva (Neith) made from a single rock and brought from Upper Egypt.

Finally a new heading opens: 'Erste Periode der Geschichte: von den frühesten Zeiten bis auf Psammetichs Alleinherrschaft, 660 a.C.' ('First period of history: from the earliest times to the sole rule of Psammetichus, 660 BC'). The text says it cannot be determined how early Egypt was cultivated or its cities founded. Around 16 centuries before Christ, Egypt already appears as a civilised people; the next page continues from here.

The only numbers are descriptive: 12 = 6 + 6 halls, 3000 = 1500 + 1500 rooms (from folio 28), 360 niches = degrees, 120 feet, 660 BC. No derivation is performed. The hand looks like a student's, more fluent and less characteristic than Gauss's own; these may be lecture notes by someone else, perhaps a family member or student, filed in the bundle.
errors: Not a mathematical error but a historical one: the 360 niches/degrees symbolism and the attribution of the Labyrinth to Menes or Psammetichus reflect late-18th-century lecture lore (Gatterer is cited on f. 28), not accurate Egyptology.
Height figures (Cheops pyramid '800 Fuß' on f. 28; an obelisk of 120 Fuß in Rome) are exaggerated or approximate. The Lateran obelisk is about 32 m, roughly 100–105 Paris feet, without its base.
The heading for Lower Egypt is numbered 'III', the same as the Obelisk heading just above it; the numbering in the notes is inconsistent.

results.what: Descriptive lecture notes on Egyptian monuments (Labyrinth, obelisks) and the start of a periodisation of Egyptian history up to Psammetichus (660 BC)
results.usually_credited_to: standard Göttingen-style universal-history lecture content (e.g. Gatterer/Heeren tradition)

deep.surprise_reason: The page has no mathematical content. It is a routine set of history lecture notes, probably not even in Gauss's hand.

checkable.asserts: The 12 halls split into 6 northern and 6 southern (cf. f. 28).
The 3000 chambers split into 1500 above and 1500 below ground (cf. f. 28).
The 12 zodiac signs of 30 degrees each give the 360 degrees matched to the 360 niches.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'die 12 Hallen' reads more like 'die 12 Pallä[ste]'/'Hallen' and ends with 'Thierkreises' (hyphenated at the margin); the sense is fine.
Line 4–5: 'und dies soll das Werk des Menes gewesen seyn'. The king's name is uncertain and should be marked [?]; 'Menes' is a guess.
Line 5–6: 'Die Nischen von oben ...[?] 360' probably reads 'Die Nischen von oben ... waren 360, dieses sind die Grade des Thierkreises'.
Obelisk passage: the duplicated 'aus einem Stück aus einem Stück' is a transcription artefact. The image reads roughly 'und waren aus [Granit/Steinen?] aus einem Stück'.
'der höchste welcher sich noch in Rom findet': 'Rom' is plausible from the image.
Lower Egypt: 'Hier war ein Tempel der Minerva, der aus einem Felsen [gehauen?], und von Ober Aegypten nach Unter Aegypten gebracht worden war'.
Last line: '16[?] Jahr[?] ...[?] vor Christi Geburt' should read '16 Jahrhunderte vor Christi Geburt' ('16 Jahrhund[erte]').
The folio number '29' appears at the top right of the image.
